bib.title: Forecasting Across Time Series Databases using Recurrent Neural Networks on Groups of Similar Series: A Clustering Approach
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:1710.03222v2 [cs.LG], 12 Sep 2018; 'Preprint submitted to Elsevier', 13 Sep 2018). The PDF prints no journal name; the repo's 'Expert Systems with Applications 2020' is not stated in this file.

question: Does training LSTMs separately on groups of similar series (found by feature-based clustering) forecast better than one global LSTM across all series in a database?
hypothesis: If a time series database is heterogeneous, a single global LSTM degrades, so building one model per subgroup of similar series should improve accuracy.
contributions: A forecasting framework that clusters series (Hyndman et al. 2015b features + Snob MML mixture model) and trains one LSTM per cluster
Preprocessing pipeline: log transform, STL deterministic deseasonalisation, sliding-window local trend normalisation, seasonal lags via input window
Evaluation on CIF2016 and NN5 under competition, fixed-origin and rolling-origin setups with non-parametric significance tests

method.summary: Series are described by 18 interpretable features (tsmeasures in R anomalous-acm), clustered with Snob (a Gaussian mixture picked by minimum message length, number of clusters chosen automatically), and each cluster gets its own peephole LSTM + affine output layer (CNTK). Each series is log-transformed, STL-deseasonalised (periodic), and trend-normalised per sliding window (MIMO strategy) before training; forecasts are denormalised and reseasonalised.
method.task: multi-step univariate time series forecasting across a database of related series

datasets.name: CIF2016
datasets.size: 72 monthly series (57 with horizon 12, 15 with horizon 6); 48 are artificially generated, the rest banking; some series have only 23 points
datasets.split: fixed origin with withheld test set (competition); last output window of train reserved for validation
datasets.preprocessing: log (log(y+1) if min(y)<=eps), STL with s.window periodic, local normalisation by last trend value in input window

datasets.name: NN5
datasets.size: 111 daily series of UK ATM cash withdrawals, 2 years
datasets.split: 56 days ahead horizon; fixed origin (competition), plus rolling origin

models.name: LSTM.Cluster
models.architecture: LSTM with peephole connections followed by affine layer without bias, size equal to output window; one model per Snob cluster
models.hidden: LSTM-cell-dimension searched in 10 to 80 (chosen value not stated)

other.CIF2016_note: clustering only applied to the 57 series with horizon 12 (need 2 full periods); the 15 horizon-6 series get one separate LSTM

models.name: LSTM.Horizon
models.architecture: same LSTM, one model per forecast horizon group (6 vs 12); CIF2016 only
models.context: inputSize 7 for outputSize 6; inputSize 15 for outputSize 12

models.name: LSTM.All
models.architecture: one global LSTM across all series, no grouping
models.context: CIF2016: inputSize 7, outputSize 12 for both horizons; NN5: 70 in, 56 out

models.name: ETS, BaggedETS, ES (smooth package), ARIMA, Naive Seasonal
models.architecture: statistical univariate; forecast package (ES from smooth); recalibrated (re-fitted) at each rolling origin

training.lr: learning-rates-per-sample searched in 0.001 to 0.04 (chosen values not stated)
training.epochs: maximum-epochs searched in 10 to 40; epoch-size ntr to ntr*3
training.regularisation: L2-regularization weight searched in 0.0005 to 0.0008; Gaussian noise injection 0.0005 to 0.005

other.hyperparameter_search: Bayesian optimisation (Snoek et al. 2012; Python bayesian-optimization package) on a validation set; ranges in Table 2; selected values not reported
other.rolling_origin: LSTM not re-fitted at each origin ('updating mode'), statistical benchmarks are re-fitted

inference.decoding: MIMO multi-output forecast over a whole output window; no recursion
inference.samples: single run per variant; no repeated seeds or ensembling reported

metrics.name: Mean MASE
metrics.definition: MAE over horizon scaled by in-sample (seasonal, period M) naive MAE; <1 beats seasonal naive

metrics.name: Median MASE / Rank MASE
metrics.definition: median and mean rank of per-series MASE

baselines: all other CIF2016 and NN5 competition entrants (Tables 3, 6)
eval.protocol: Three setups: competition (CO, fixed origin, Mean sMAPE vs original entrants), fixed origin (FO, with significance testing), rolling origin (RO, benchmarks re-fitted per origin). Significance: aligned Friedman rank-sum with Hochberg post-hoc (on sMAPE) for multiple methods, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank for two methods, alpha=0.05.

availability.data: CIF2016 and NN5 public competition datasets

evidence.quote: The statistical testing is done using the sMAPE measure.

results.claim: On NN5 rolling origin (111 ATM series), LSTM.Cluster has Mean MASE 0.93 versus 0.95 for ungrouped LSTM.All; the exponential smoothing methods ES and ETS score 0.87.
results.baseline_value: LSTM.All 0.95; ES 0.87; ETS 0.87; BaggedETS 0.88; ARIMA 0.96; Naive Seasonal 1.10
results.setup: NN5, 111 daily ATM series, 56-day horizon, rolling origin (RO), LSTM not re-fitted, benchmarks re-fitted
results.table: Table 8, column Mean MASE, rows LSTM.Cluster 0.93, LSTM.All 0.95, ES 0.87, ETS 0.87
results.note: This is the likely source of the '0.93 vs 0.95, 0.87' figures. The 0.87 belongs to ES (smooth package) and ETS, not to 'simple exponential smoothing' (SES); the paper never uses the term SES for a benchmark.

results.claim: NN5 fixed origin Mean MASE: LSTM.Cluster 0.94, LSTM.All 0.96, ES and ETS 0.86.
results.table: Table 7, column Mean MASE, rows LSTM.Cluster 0.94, LSTM.All 0.96, ES 0.86

results.claim: NN5 fixed-origin Mean sMAPE: ES 21.44, ETS 21.46, LSTM.Cluster 21.66, LSTM.All 23.46.
results.table: Table 7, column Mean sMAPE, rows LSTM.Cluster 21.66, LSTM.All 23.46, ES 21.44

results.claim: NN5 rolling-origin Mean sMAPE: ES 22.18, ETS 22.24, LSTM.Cluster 23.38, LSTM.All 23.89.
results.table: Table 8, column Mean sMAPE, rows LSTM.Cluster 23.38, LSTM.All 23.89, ES 22.18

results.claim: In the NN5 competition setup LSTM.Cluster scores Mean sMAPE 21.6 (6th overall), LSTM.All 23.4; the winner (Wildi) scored 19.9.
results.quote: It can be seen that the proposed LSTM.Cluster variant performs better than the LSTM.All variant, and reaches a 6th overall rank.

results.claim: On NN5, LSTM.Cluster beats LSTM.All significantly (paired Wilcoxon p = 7.22e-4), but neither beats the exponential smoothing benchmarks.
results.setup: NN5, LSTM.Cluster vs LSTM.All, sMAPE, alpha 0.05; the paper does not say whether FO or RO forecasts were used
results.quote:
The paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives an overall p-value of 7.22 × 10−4, within the
two LSTM variants.

results.claim: NN5 post-hoc test with ETS as control: LSTM.Cluster is not significantly worse than ETS (pHoch 0.233) while LSTM.All is (5.03e-8).
results.setup: NN5, aligned Friedman (overall p 6.59 × 10−11) on sMAPE, control = ETS
results.note: Not significantly worse is not evidence of equal or better: LSTM.Cluster never beats ETS on any NN5 measure.

results.claim: On CIF2016 competition setup LSTM.Cluster has the lowest Mean sMAPE of all entrants (10.53) versus LSTM.All 10.69 and ETS 11.87.
results.table: Table 3, column Mean sMAPE, row LSTM.Cluster 10.53

results.claim: On CIF2016 Mean MASE LSTM.Cluster (0.89) is worse than ungrouped LSTM.All (0.83); on Median sMAPE and Rank measures BaggedETS/ETS and LSTM.All lead.
results.baseline_value: LSTM.All 0.83; LSTM and ETS combo 0.79; BaggedETS 0.83
results.table: Table 3, column Mean MASE, rows LSTM.Cluster 0.89, LSTM.All 0.83
results.note: Authors: 'the results change quite drastically, and traditional univariate methods such as BaggedETS often outperform our methods'.

results.claim: On CIF2016 there is no significant difference among the LSTM variants (aligned Friedman p = 0.8010).
results.metric: aligned Friedman overall p-value, LSTM variants
results.quote:
the corresponding aligned Friedman test has an overall p-value
of 0.8010, which highlights that these diﬀerences are insigniﬁcant
results.note: This is the 'no significant difference on another dataset' result.

results.claim: CIF2016 post-hoc: with BaggedETS as control, LSTM.Cluster (pHoch 0.092) and LSTM.All (0.216) are not significantly worse; LSTM.Horizon is borderline (0.048).
results.setup: CIF2016 vs original entrants, overall Friedman p 7.84 × 10−6
results.note: Text says LSTM.All and LSTM.Cluster are not worse than control.

results.claim: CIF2016 rolling origin: LSTM.Horizon has the best Mean sMAPE (9.80), LSTM.Cluster 9.95, ETS 10.76, LSTM.All 11.10; BaggedETS wins every other measure.
results.table: Table 5, column Mean sMAPE, row LSTM.Horizon 9.80

limits: Only two datasets (CIF2016, NN5); no M3: authors exclude it because its series are not similar.
CIF2016 contains 48 artificial series 'that may not contain useful cross-series information'; the authors attribute BaggedETS wins on other measures to this.
On CIF2016 the clustering only applies to the 57 horizon-12 series (STL needs 2 full periods); the 15 horizon-6 series use a separate model.
On NN5 the cluster LSTM never beats ES/ETS/BaggedETS on any measure; non-significance versus ETS only means not shown worse.
Significance testing uses sMAPE only; on CIF2016 the three LSTM variants are not significantly different from each other (p 0.8010), so the 10.53 vs 10.69 gap is not significant.
NN5 original entrants' forecasts are unavailable, so significance vs the competition winners is untested.
Rolling-origin LSTMs are not re-fitted while benchmarks are, a asymmetry the authors note for cost.
Selected hyperparameters, seeds, run counts, hardware and training time are not reported; code is not mentioned.
Input window heuristic would suit poorly daily data with yearly seasonality (authors' remark); deseasonalisation applied to all series regardless.
Dated: LSTM only (CNTK, now discontinued); no transformer or later M4/N-BEATS-style comparisons.

terms.definition: proposed method: one LSTM per cluster of series found by feature extraction + Snob
baseline LSTM: one global model across all series in the dataset
CIF2016 variant grouping series by required forecast horizon (6 vs 12)
